title: Rescue the Perishing, and the Slacker's Field
summary: The words of the wise conclude with sayings about envy of the wicked, the house that wisdom builds, the duty to rescue those being led to death, and the danger of gloating over a fallen enemy. A second short collection, also called sayings of the wise, adds counsel on fair judgment, honest words, and refusing revenge, and ends with a scene: a teacher walks past a neglected field and draws a lesson about laziness.
story: This chapter closes the section of Proverbs attributed to the wise (22:17 to 24:22) and adds a brief appendix (24:23-34), before the book returns to Solomon's sayings in chapter 25. The themes are familiar from earlier chapters: the wicked seem to prosper, the lazy sleep while their fields decay, and wisdom proves more powerful than strength. What is new is the moral urgency of verses 10 to 12. The wise are not only told to avoid evil but to act when others are in danger, and they are warned that pleading ignorance won't satisfy the God who weighs hearts.
historical:
The first half of the chapter continues the collection that most scholars link to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, though the close parallels are concentrated in chapters 22 and 23. Verse 23 opens a separate, shorter collection with its own heading, showing again that Proverbs was compiled from several sources by editors who marked the joins. Verses 21 and 22 place loyalty to the king beside the fear of the LORD, reflecting the setting of a monarchy in which royal officials were trained in wisdom and rebellion was both a political and a moral danger.

The scene in verses 30 to 34 assumes the farming life of Judah's hill country, where terraced fields and vineyards were held in by walls of fieldstone. Left untended for a few seasons, such a plot would be overrun by thorns, and its walls would slump and fall. The closing lines repeat almost word for word a saying from Proverbs 6:10-11, one of several places where the book's collections share material.
cultural:
Justice in an Israelite town was done at the gate, where elders heard cases and witnesses gave testimony. That setting stands behind verses 23 to 28: showing partiality in judgment, declaring the guilty innocent, and testifying against a neighbor without cause were the ways a community's justice was corrupted. A judge who called the guilty innocent would be cursed by peoples and nations, because everyone depends on honest courts. The honest answer of verse 26 is compared to a kiss on the lips, likely a sign of close friendship and loyalty in that culture, as greetings with a kiss were common among family and friends.

Verse 29 addresses the ancient instinct for payback. Blood feuds and retaliation were widespread, and while Israel's law set limits on punishment, the private urge to repay a wrong was strong. The wise are told to refuse it, leaving repayment to God, the one who repays a man according to his deeds (verse 12).
literary: The chapter mixes several forms. Verses 3 and 4 are a small building poem in which wisdom, understanding, and knowledge build, establish, and fill a house. Verses 10 to 12 are a pointed address with rhetorical questions that anticipate an excuse and answer it. Verses 13 and 14 use an extended comparison: as honey is sweet to the taste, so wisdom is sweet to the soul. The final section (verses 30 to 34) is a first-person observation story, rare in Proverbs, in which the teacher reports what he saw, what he thought, and the lesson he received. The repeated phrase “a little” in verse 33 imitates the small, reasonable-sounding delays that add up to ruin.

outline.t: Rescue those being led to death
The righteous rise again; do not gloat, fret, or rebel
Further sayings of the wise: justice, honesty, no revenge

doctrines.note: God weighs hearts and repays each person according to his deeds (verse 12). No one can hide behind the claim not to have known, and the refusal to take revenge in verse 29 rests on trust that God judges justly.
Wisdom builds a house and fills it with treasure, and it is stronger than brute strength (verses 3 to 6). It is also sweet: not a burden to be endured but something to be enjoyed like honey.
The chapter names sins of commission (plotting evil, false testimony, revenge) and sins of omission: failing to rescue the perishing and letting a field go to ruin through neglect.

words.note: Natsal, to rescue or deliver, often used of snatching someone out of danger. In verse 11 the command is active and urgent: rescue those being led away to death. The same verb describes God's great acts of deliverance, and here the wise are called to share in that work.

Takan, to weigh or measure. God is the one who weighs hearts (verse 12), a picture that also appears earlier in Proverbs. It may echo the Egyptian image of a heart weighed in judgment, but in Proverbs the weigher is the living LORD, who sees motives that human courts cannot.

Atsel, sluggish or lazy, the book's recurring figure of the slacker. He is not presented as wicked in a dramatic way, only as someone who keeps postponing. The scene in verses 30 to 34 shows that his ruin comes gradually and then all at once.

Acharit, the end or the future. Verses 14 and 20 contrast the future of the one who finds wisdom, whose hope will not be cut off, with the evil man, who has no future. Proverbs repeatedly teaches readers to judge a path by where it ends.

christ: The call to rescue those being led to death echoes through Scripture and takes its fullest shape in Jesus, who came to seek and to save the lost, and who warned in his parable of the sheep and the goats that people will be judged by how they treated the hungry, the stranger, and the prisoner. Verses 17 and 18, which forbid gloating over a fallen enemy, and verse 29, which forbids repaying evil for evil, look toward Jesus' teaching to love enemies and Paul's command not to repay evil for evil but to leave room for God's judgment. The link is one of continuity in ethics: Proverbs lays down the pattern that Jesus deepens and embodies when he prays for those who crucify him.

hard.q: Does verse 16 promise that good people always recover from disaster?
hard.a: Verse 16 says that though a righteous man may fall seven times, he still gets up, while the wicked stumble in bad times. It is easy to read this as a guarantee that the righteous always bounce back. But it is a proverb, and a proverb describes how life usually goes under God, not a promise for every case. Seven is a number of fullness, so the point is resilience: the righteous are knocked down again and again and are not finished, because God upholds them. Other parts of Scripture, especially Job, Ecclesiastes, and the lament psalms, speak honestly of righteous people who suffer long and die without visible recovery. Read together, the Bible holds both truths: God sustains his people, and his sustaining does not always look like restored fortunes in this life. The New Testament places the final rising of the righteous in the resurrection.

questions: Verse 12 anticipates the excuse, we did not know. Where might you be choosing not to know about someone's danger?
Why do you think Proverbs warns against gloating over an enemy's fall, even when the enemy deserved it?
The slacker's ruin came through a little sleep and a little slumber. What small delay in your life is quietly letting the walls fall down?
